context: A Customer Support Resolution Agent returns malformed JSON from process_refund on 7% of calls. The current tool error response contains only a single string: 'REFUND_ERROR'. Downstream validation code cannot determine whether to retry the call, escalate, or log the error — engineers manually triage 50+ errors daily at a cost of 2.5 engineering hours per day.
stem: Which error response structure would best allow automated downstream handling of process_refund failures?
optionA: Return a numeric error code (1=retryable, 2=non-retryable, 3=escalate) mapped to documentation.
optionB: Return a three-field object: errorCategory (string classifying the error type), isRetryable (boolean), and description (human-readable explanation).
optionC: Return an HTTP-style status code (500 for server errors, 400 for client errors) with the original error string.
optionD: Return a nested error object containing the full stack trace, timestamp, and raw database error for maximum diagnostic detail.
whyCorrect: The three-field structured error (errorCategory + isRetryable boolean + human-readable description) is the canonical structured tool error format. The isRetryable boolean directly enables automated retry/escalate/log decisions without documentation lookups or manual triage.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — a numeric code requires documentation mapping; the isRetryable boolean in the three-field format is semantically self-documenting and directly machine-actionable.
whyWrongC: This is the partial-correct trap — HTTP status codes are a web convention that don't map cleanly to tool-call error semantics and still require interpretation logic.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — full stack traces are appropriate for logging, not for machine-readable automated decision-making by downstream code.
examTrap: partial-correct: uses alternative error structure instead of the canonical three-field format

context: A team shares a project-level MCP server for a proprietary database via a .mcp.json file in the repository root. A new developer reports the MCP server is unavailable in their Claude Code session despite cloning the repository. Investigation reveals the developer's ~/.claude.json has no MCP entries, and the developer ran Claude Code from their home directory (~/) instead of the project root.
stem: What is the correct action to make the shared MCP server available to the new developer?
optionA: Copy the .mcp.json server configuration entry into the developer's ~/.claude.json mcpServers section.
optionB: Ask a project administrator to register the MCP server in the organization's central Claude configuration registry.
optionC: Have the developer run Claude Code from the project root directory so .mcp.json is automatically detected and loaded.
optionD: Add the developer's machine hostname to an allowedHosts field in the .mcp.json configuration to grant access.
whyCorrect: .mcp.json is a project-level configuration file — Claude Code loads it automatically when invoked from the directory containing it. Running from ~/ instead of the project root means .mcp.json is never detected. No configuration changes are needed.
whyWrongA: This is the mcp-level trap — copying to ~/.claude.json makes a personal user-level copy instead of using the shared project-level .mcp.json, undermining the team-sharing design.
whyWrongB: This is the mcp-level trap — no organization-level central Claude configuration registry exists; .mcp.json in the project root is the shared configuration mechanism.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — no allowedHosts field exists in .mcp.json; the issue is simply running Claude Code from the wrong directory.

context: A Structured Data Extraction pipeline uses tool_choice: 'auto' to optionally invoke an extraction tool. Business requirements change: every document submission must now produce structured output — free-text responses with no tool call are no longer acceptable. In the past week, 23 of 1,000 submissions returned free-text responses because the model determined no tool call was necessary.
stem: Which tool_choice setting ensures the model always calls a tool on every document submission?
optionA: tool_choice: 'required' — forces the model to call at least one tool in every response.
optionB: tool_choice: 'auto' with a system prompt instruction 'You must always call the extraction tool' — the model will comply.
optionC: tool_choice: 'any' — forces the model to call at least one of the available tools in every response.
optionD: tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'extract_fields'} — forces the model to call specifically the extract_fields tool in every response.
whyCorrect: tool_choice 'any' forces the model to call at least one available tool — it cannot return a free-text-only response. This eliminates the 23 free-text responses. 'auto' allows the model to skip tool calls, which is the current behavior causing the problem.
whyWrongA: This is the any-vs-auto trap — 'required' is not a valid tool_choice value in the Claude API; the valid values are 'auto', 'any', and the specific tool object.
whyWrongB: This is the compliance-prompt trap — 'auto' with a prompt instruction is probabilistic; the 23 failures demonstrate the model already skips tool calls despite presumably being instructed to extract.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — forcing the specific extract_fields tool works but is overly prescriptive; 'any' is the appropriate choice when any tool call is sufficient.
examTrap: any-vs-auto: confuses tool_choice 'any' (forces any tool call) with 'auto' (model may skip)

context: A Multi-Agent Research System has 8 available tools: web_search, search_arxiv, search_pubmed, search_news, analyze_pdf, analyze_html, analyze_csv, synthesize. The research coordinator miscalls search_arxiv on general web queries 34% of the time and uses web_search on academic paper queries 28% of the time. Tool descriptions currently read: web_search: 'Search the web', search_arxiv: 'Search academic papers.'
stem: Which intervention most directly reduces tool misrouting between web_search and search_arxiv?
optionA: Add an intent classifier that detects query type (general vs. academic) before the tool call and routes to the correct tool.
optionB: Expand the tool descriptions to include explicit use cases, source types, and examples: web_search for current events and general knowledge; search_arxiv for peer-reviewed preprints and academic research.
optionC: Set tool_choice to 'any' to let the model pick from available tools based on query content.
optionD: Create a wrapper tool 'smart_search' that internally calls both web_search and search_arxiv and merges results to eliminate routing decisions.
whyCorrect: Tool descriptions ARE the primary tool selection mechanism. The current one-line descriptions lack specificity — 'Search the web' and 'Search academic papers' are ambiguous. Expanded descriptions with explicit use cases and examples give the model the semantic information needed to route correctly without adding classification infrastructure.
whyWrongA: This is the misrouting-fix trap — adding a routing classifier is premature complexity when improving tool descriptions is the correct first intervention for misrouting.
whyWrongC: This is the any-vs-auto trap — tool_choice 'any' forces a call but doesn't influence which tool is selected; the model still needs description quality to route correctly.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — merging tools eliminates routing but loses the specificity of academic-indexed search and increases per-query cost unnecessarily.
examTrap: misrouting-fix: adds routing classifier instead of expanding tool descriptions first

context: A Customer Support Resolution Agent uses lookup_order to retrieve order details. On 8% of calls, lookup_order returns an empty array because the order is in a pending state not yet replicated to the query database — this is a transient consistency lag of 2-4 seconds. The current retry logic retries any empty response 3 times with 1-second intervals ($0.0015 per retry), adding $180/month in unnecessary costs for 120,000 monthly calls.
stem: How should the lookup_order tool's error response be structured to allow the calling agent to correctly distinguish transient empty-due-to-lag from legitimate not-found responses?
optionA: Return null instead of [] for not-found cases so the agent can retry [] (lag) but not null (confirmed not-found).
optionB: Return the three-field structured error for failures, and include a resultStatus field ('pending_replication' vs 'confirmed_not_found') in the response envelope for empty results.
optionC: Add a cache-control header to the tool response indicating freshness so the agent can decide whether to retry.
optionD: Increase the retry delay from 1 second to 5 seconds so the replication lag resolves before the second attempt.
whyCorrect: The three-field error structure handles failure cases. For empty results, a resultStatus field distinguishing 'pending_replication' (retryable) from 'confirmed_not_found' (not retryable) gives the agent a programmatic basis for retry decisions — eliminating unnecessary retries on legitimate not-found cases.
whyWrongA: This is the empty-result trap — using null vs. [] as a semantic signal is fragile and non-standard; the structured resultStatus field is explicit and machine-readable.
whyWrongC: This is the partial-correct trap — cache-control headers are an HTTP web concept; tool responses use structured JSON fields, not HTTP headers.
whyWrongD: This is the empty-result trap — increasing retry delay reduces collision with lag but still retries confirmed not-found cases unnecessarily, not eliminating the $180/month waste.
examTrap: empty-result: retries all empty results instead of classifying retryable vs. non-retryable

context: A development team runs a private MCP server exposing internal code review tools. The server configuration is stored in each developer's ~/.claude.json. A new developer joins the team and receives onboarding instructions to manually add the MCP configuration to their ~/.claude.json. Six months later, the team updates the MCP server URL — 4 developers still have the old URL cached in their personal configs and report broken tool access for 3 days.
stem: What configuration change would prevent this class of synchronization failure for shared team MCP servers?
optionA: Migrate the shared MCP server configuration from ~/.claude.json to a .mcp.json file in the project repository root so it is version-controlled and automatically updated via git pull.
optionB: Create a Makefile target 'make update-mcp' that developers run to sync their ~/.claude.json from a central template.
optionC: Add the MCP server URL to the project's .env file and reference it from CLAUDE.md to ensure consistency.
optionD: Store the MCP configuration in the repository's CI/CD environment variables so it propagates to all developer machines.
whyCorrect: .mcp.json in the project root is version-controlled and shared — when the URL changes, a single commit updates it for all developers via git pull. Personal ~/.claude.json entries are independent copies that diverge over time, as the 4-developer URL mismatch demonstrates.
whyWrongB: This is the mcp-level trap — a Makefile target still requires individual action and doesn't solve the root problem of decentralized personal configs; it just adds a manual sync step.
whyWrongC: This is the mcp-level trap — MCP server configuration belongs in .mcp.json, not CLAUDE.md or .env; the format and loading mechanism are distinct.
whyWrongD: This is the mcp-level trap — CI/CD environment variables are for pipeline processes, not for developer machine Claude Code configuration.
examTrap: mcp-level: keeps configuration in personal ~/.claude.json instead of project-level .mcp.json

context: A Structured Data Extraction pipeline for tax forms must call a mandatory audit_log tool on every extraction — regulators require a record that every form was processed. The pipeline currently uses tool_choice: 'auto'. In an audit sample of 10,000 forms, 67 records show no audit_log call was made — the model skipped it when extracted data was trivially simple, determining the log was unnecessary.
stem: Which tool_choice configuration guarantees audit_log is called on every single extraction?
optionA: tool_choice: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'audit_log'} — forces the model to call audit_log specifically on every response.
optionB: tool_choice: 'any' with a system prompt instruction 'Always call audit_log for compliance' — together these ensure the tool is called.
optionC: tool_choice: 'auto' with the audit_log description updated to include 'MANDATORY: must be called on every form extraction.'
optionD: tool_choice: 'required' — forces any tool call, which given audit_log is listed first, will always select it.
whyCorrect: {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'audit_log'} forces the model to call the specific audit_log tool on every response with zero ambiguity. This is the only configuration that provides a 100% deterministic guarantee that the specific required tool is called.
whyWrongB: This is the compliance-prompt trap — 'any' forces some tool call but not specifically audit_log; combined with a prompt it's still probabilistic about which tool is called first.
whyWrongC: This is the compliance-prompt trap — 'auto' with a description update remains probabilistic; the 67 misses prove the model already skips it despite presumably having context about compliance.
whyWrongD: This is the any-vs-auto trap — 'required' is not a valid tool_choice value; tool ordering does not determine selection under 'any' either.
examTrap: any-vs-auto: confuses forced-specific-tool with 'any' or invalid values

context: A developer configures Claude Code with a Read-only file analysis MCP server for security (no write access). The server is configured in the developer's ~/.claude.json. When the developer shares their analysis workflow with a colleague, the colleague's Claude Code session lacks the MCP server entirely. The colleague clones the project repo — no .mcp.json is present in the repository.
stem: What should the developer do to share the MCP server configuration with the colleague without compromising the intended read-only security posture?
optionA: Send the colleague the exact JSON configuration to manually add to their ~/.claude.json.
optionB: Add the read-only MCP server configuration to a .mcp.json file in the project repository root and commit it; team members automatically get it via the repository.
optionC: Grant the colleague read access to the developer's home directory so they can copy the ~/.claude.json file directly.
optionD: Create a setup script that programmatically writes the MCP configuration to the colleague's ~/.claude.json on first run.
whyCorrect: .mcp.json is the project-level, version-controlled, shared MCP configuration. Adding the read-only server to .mcp.json in the repo root makes it available to all team members via git clone/pull without any manual configuration copying. The read-only security posture is preserved in the server's own access controls.
whyWrongA: This is the mcp-level trap — manually sending JSON for ~/.claude.json is the exact fragile personal-config-sharing pattern that .mcp.json is designed to replace.
whyWrongC: This is the mcp-level trap — sharing home directory access is a security anti-pattern; ~/.claude.json is personal and may contain other sensitive configurations.
whyWrongD: This is the mcp-level trap — programmatically writing to personal config files is the same fragile approach as manual copying, with added automation complexity.
examTrap: mcp-level: uses personal ~/.claude.json sharing instead of project-level .mcp.json

context: A Structured Data Extraction system processes bank statements using a validation-retry loop. The tool schema defines 12 required fields. On the first extraction attempt, 9 fields are populated and 3 are null. The retry loop fires and submits the same document again — 9 fields are populated and 3 are null again, identical to the first attempt. The loop retries 5 more times at $0.012 per attempt ($0.084 total per document), wasting $420/month across 5,000 monthly documents.
stem: What retry logic change would eliminate the wasteful retries on this class of failure?
optionA: Increase the retry count from 5 to 10, as persistent empty fields may resolve on later attempts with more compute.
optionB: After the first retry returns identical results, classify the failure as a structural extraction limit (not a transient error) and abort the retry loop — flagging the document for human review instead.
optionC: Change tool_choice from 'auto' to 'any' to force a different tool selection on retries, potentially recovering the 3 missing fields.
optionD: Reduce the 12 required fields to 9 to match what the extraction tool reliably produces, eliminating null field failures.
whyCorrect: When a retry returns identical results, the failure is structural — not transient. Retrying a structural extraction limit is the empty-result trap: no additional retries will recover data that the document doesn't contain or the tool can't extract. Abort and flag for human review.
whyWrongA: This is the empty-result trap — increasing retries on a structurally identical failure multiplies waste; if the second attempt is identical to the first, subsequent attempts will be too.
whyWrongC: This is the any-vs-auto trap — tool_choice affects whether a tool is called, not which data fields can be recovered from the source document.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — reducing required fields changes the data contract and may mask legitimate data quality issues in the source documents.
examTrap: empty-result: retries on a structural extraction limit instead of classifying and escalating

context: A Multi-Agent Research System uses an MCP server for document analysis. The server is configured in .mcp.json. A new research analyst joins the team, clones the repository, and opens Claude Code. The analyst reports that document analysis tools show 'server unavailable' in their session. The analyst's session was launched from a personal projects folder, not the cloned repository directory.
stem: What is the correct diagnosis and fix for the analyst's missing MCP server access?
optionA: The .mcp.json is corrupted; the analyst should delete and recreate it from the team's configuration template.
optionB: The MCP server needs to be registered globally in the organization's Claude Code admin panel to ensure availability regardless of launch directory.
optionC: The analyst must launch Claude Code from the cloned repository directory so that .mcp.json in the project root is detected and loaded.
optionD: The analyst's OS user account lacks permissions to read .mcp.json; an admin must grant file system access.
whyCorrect: .mcp.json is loaded relative to the working directory where Claude Code is launched. Launching from a personal projects folder means the project-root .mcp.json is not in scope. No server registration or config changes are needed — just run Claude Code from the correct directory.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — the .mcp.json is not corrupted; other team members can use it fine. The issue is the launch directory.
whyWrongB: This is the mcp-level trap — no organization-level Claude Code admin panel for MCP exists; .mcp.json in the project root is the intended sharing mechanism.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — file permissions would produce a read error, not 'server unavailable'; the symptom points to the file not being found due to wrong working directory.
examTrap: mcp-level: assumes global registration or admin action is needed instead of directory-relative .mcp.json loading

context: A Customer Support Resolution Agent's get_customer tool is being called 1,800 times/hour — 3.2x the expected rate of 560/hour. Call sampling shows 42% of calls are for customers whose profiles were already retrieved in the same session less than 90 seconds prior. The tool description reads: 'Retrieves customer profile and account information. Call whenever customer data is needed.'
stem: What single change would most reduce redundant get_customer calls without requiring code changes to the agent loop?
optionA: Add a rate limiter to the get_customer tool endpoint to block calls exceeding 1,000/hour.
optionB: Update the get_customer tool description to specify: 'Call only when customer profile is not already available in the current context. Do not call again if data was already retrieved in this session.'
optionC: Set tool_choice to {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'lookup_order'} to force the agent to use lookup_order as its first call.
optionD: Add a system-level cache TTL of 5 minutes on get_customer responses to automatically dedup calls at the infrastructure layer.
whyCorrect: Tool descriptions ARE the tool selection mechanism. The current description 'Call whenever customer data is needed' actively encourages redundant calls. Updating it to specify 'not available in current context' and 'do not call again if already retrieved' gives the model explicit, semantically actionable guidance without code changes.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — rate limiting at the tool level degrades agent performance and causes tool failures when the limit is hit; it doesn't address the root cause of redundant calls.
whyWrongC: This is the any-vs-auto trap — forcing lookup_order doesn't reduce get_customer calls; it changes the first call but doesn't address repeated get_customer invocations.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — infrastructure caching reduces the cost per call but doesn't reduce the number of redundant tool invocations consuming agent context and latency budget.
examTrap: misrouting-fix: addresses tool routing at infrastructure or configuration level instead of improving the tool description

context: A developer's personal Claude Code configuration in ~/.claude.json includes a sensitive internal API key for a private MCP linting server. The developer commits .mcp.json to the project repository, not realizing they accidentally included the API key inline in the .mcp.json content. 48 hours later, the repository's secret scanning alerts on the committed key. 6 team members have pulled the repo during this window.
stem: What configuration practice would have prevented this key exposure?
optionA: Store the API key as an environment variable and reference it via a ${ENV_VAR} placeholder in .mcp.json rather than inlining the key value.
optionB: Use ~/.claude.json exclusively for all MCP configurations to prevent project-level files from being committed to version control.
optionC: Encrypt the .mcp.json file before committing using AES-256 so team members must decrypt it locally.
optionD: Add .mcp.json to .gitignore to prevent it from being committed, and distribute it through a separate secure channel.
whyCorrect: Storing secrets inline in any version-controlled file is always incorrect. The correct practice is to store sensitive values as environment variables and reference them via placeholders in .mcp.json. This allows .mcp.json to be safely committed while keeping secrets out of the repository.
whyWrongB: This is the mcp-level trap — using only ~/.claude.json for all MCP configs defeats the team-sharing benefit of .mcp.json and doesn't prevent secret exposure if the key is still stored insecurely.
whyWrongC: This is the partial-correct trap — encrypting the file adds complexity and prevents readable review; environment variable references are the standard secure and usable approach.
whyWrongD: This is the mcp-level trap — .gitignoring .mcp.json removes the team-sharing benefit; the correct solution separates the non-secret config (committable) from secret values (environment variables).
examTrap: mcp-level: avoids project-level .mcp.json instead of using environment variables for secrets

context: A Structured Data Extraction pipeline processes 3,000 financial reports daily with custom_id values for result tracking. The pipeline uses tool_choice: 'auto'. On 4.1% of reports (123/day), the model returns a free-text explanation instead of calling the extraction tool — typically when the document contains a disclaimer page as its first page. These 123 daily misses require manual re-processing at a cost of $0.50 per document ($61.50/day).
stem: What is the most targeted fix for the 4.1% miss rate where the model skips the extraction tool on disclaimer-first documents?
optionA: Add a pre-processing step that strips disclaimer pages from documents before submitting to the extraction pipeline.
optionB: Change tool_choice from 'auto' to 'any' so the model is required to call at least one tool on every document, eliminating free-text-only responses.
optionC: Update the extraction tool description to explicitly state it should be called even when the document begins with a disclaimer or non-data page.
optionD: Increase the model's temperature to 0.0 for deterministic extraction that always follows the same tool-calling pattern.
whyCorrect: tool_choice 'any' forces the model to call at least one available tool — it cannot return free-text only. This directly eliminates the 4.1% miss rate caused by the model choosing not to call the extraction tool when it encounters disclaimer-first documents.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — stripping disclaimers reduces misses on this class but doesn't fix the underlying tool_choice setting; new non-data page types would still cause misses.
whyWrongC: This is the compliance-prompt trap — description updates improve routing semantics but remain probabilistic; 'any' provides a deterministic structural guarantee.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — temperature affects response sampling variation; it does not guarantee tool calls under tool_choice 'auto' when the model determines no tool is appropriate.
examTrap: any-vs-auto: uses description or temperature instead of changing tool_choice from 'auto' to 'any'

context: A Multi-Agent Research System's analyze_document tool fails silently: when a document cannot be parsed, it returns {'status': 'ok', 'content': null} instead of an error. The synthesis agent receives null content and generates a summary stating 'no relevant information found.' Quality reviewers find 11% of research reports contain fabricated summaries based on null content, with $2,800/month in rework costs.
stem: Which error response design change to analyze_document would allow the synthesis agent to correctly handle parse failures?
optionA: Return {'status': 'error', 'message': 'parse failed'} to distinguish failures from successful empty results.
optionB: Return a three-field structured error: errorCategory ('parse_failure'), isRetryable (false for structural failures, true for transient I/O errors), and description with actionable detail.
optionC: Throw an exception in the tool implementation so the agent framework automatically re-routes to a backup analysis tool.
optionD: Return {'status': 'ok', 'content': '', 'parseError': true} to preserve backward compatibility while signaling the failure.
whyCorrect: The three-field structured error (errorCategory + isRetryable + description) is the canonical tool error format. isRetryable correctly distinguishes transient I/O failures (worth retrying) from structural parse failures (not retryable). This gives the synthesis agent programmatic decision-making capability rather than needing to interpret ambiguous fields.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — {'status': 'error', 'message': 'parse failed'} is better than null but lacks the isRetryable field needed for automated retry logic.
whyWrongC: This is the partial-correct trap — throwing exceptions exposes implementation details to the agent framework; structured error responses in the tool return value are the correct pattern.
whyWrongD: This is the partial-correct trap — a mixed {'status': 'ok', 'parseError': true} is semantically contradictory and requires the caller to check multiple fields rather than a standardized error structure.
examTrap: partial-correct: uses alternative error structure instead of the three-field canonical format with isRetryable

context: An engineer uses Claude Code with 14 MCP tools across 3 servers. During a debugging session, the model calls a local_file_read tool 8 times on the same file path and a database_query tool 4 times with identical parameters — no tool results changed between identical calls. Session logs show the model has no explicit instruction about caching or result reuse. The redundant calls add 12 seconds of latency and $0.04 per session.
stem: What tool description change would most directly reduce redundant calls to idempotent read tools?
optionA: Add 'Results are cached for 60 seconds; do not call again within this window' to the description of each idempotent tool.
optionB: Implement server-side caching in the MCP server that returns cached results for repeated identical calls silently.
optionC: Set tool_choice to {'type': 'tool', 'name': 'local_file_read'} to restrict the model to one tool type, reducing the total call volume.
optionD: Add 'This tool returns deterministic results for identical inputs within a session. If you have already called this tool with the same parameters, use the previously obtained result rather than calling again.' to each idempotent tool's description.
whyCorrect: Tool descriptions guide model behavior. Explicitly instructing the model that results are deterministic for identical parameters and to reuse prior results directly targets the redundant call behavior. This is the tool description as the selection/usage mechanism principle applied to idempotent tool usage.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — a 60-second cache TTL hint is vague and time-based rather than semantically describing the idempotent nature and instructing result reuse.
whyWrongB: This is the partial-correct trap — server-side caching reduces cost per call but does not reduce the number of redundant tool calls consuming agent context and latency budget.
whyWrongC: This is the any-vs-auto trap — forcing a specific tool doesn't reduce repeated calls to it; it just restricts which tool can be called.
examTrap: misrouting-fix: addresses redundancy at infrastructure level instead of tool description guidance

context: A Structured Data Extraction pipeline processes medical records in batches of 1,000 using the Batch API with custom_id for result correlation. Engineers want to implement a multi-turn validation workflow: extract fields (turn 1), validate against a reference database (turn 2), and resolve discrepancies (turn 3) — all within a single batch job. The team assumes the Batch API supports this chained tool-calling conversation.
stem: What is wrong with the team's assumption about using the Batch API for the 3-turn validation workflow?
optionA: The Batch API limits each job to a maximum of 2 tool calls per item, making a 3-turn workflow impossible.
optionB: The Batch API does not support multi-turn conversations — each batch item is a single request/response pair. A 3-turn workflow requires a real-time synchronous API or custom orchestration outside the Batch API.
optionC: The Batch API requires a premium tier subscription to process medical records due to HIPAA compliance constraints.
optionD: The Batch API supports multi-turn tool calling but only when custom_id fields are used for conversation threading.
whyCorrect: The Batch API processes each item as a single, independent request/response pair — it does not support multi-turn conversations or chained tool calls. The 3-turn validation workflow requires either a synchronous Messages API with a conversation loop or a custom orchestration layer outside the Batch API.
whyWrongA: This is the batch-multiturn trap — the actual constraint is no multi-turn support at all, not a 2-call limit.
whyWrongC: This is the partial-correct trap — HIPAA compliance is an organizational concern; the Batch API itself has no medical-record-specific tier restrictions.
whyWrongD: This is the batch-multiturn trap — custom_id is for result correlation only; it does not enable multi-turn conversation threading within a single batch job.
examTrap: batch-multiturn: claims Batch API supports multi-turn tool calling with the right parameters

context: A Customer Support Resolution Agent is deployed with 5 tools. Post-launch analysis reveals escalate_to_human is called in 31% of tickets — nearly triple the expected 11%. Sampling shows the model escalates when it encounters any order status other than 'delivered' or 'cancelled', even for 'in_transit' tickets that lookup_order can resolve with a tracking update. The escalate_to_human description reads: 'Escalates cases the agent cannot resolve.'
stem: What change would most reduce the 31% escalation rate back toward the expected 11%?
optionA: Remove escalate_to_human from the agent's allowedTools list during off-hours to force automation-only resolution.
optionB: Add a routing classifier that checks order status before the agent acts, blocking escalation for 'in_transit' status codes.
optionC: Update lookup_order's description to enumerate which order statuses it can resolve (including 'in_transit' with tracking updates) and update escalate_to_human's description to specify it is for cases where lookup_order or process_refund cannot achieve resolution.
optionD: Switch tool_choice to 'any' to ensure the agent always calls a resolution tool before falling back to escalation.
whyCorrect: Tool descriptions ARE the selection mechanism. lookup_order's description doesn't convey that it handles 'in_transit' cases; escalate_to_human's description 'cases the agent cannot resolve' is too broad. Expanding both descriptions with specific conditions reduces ambiguous escalation without architectural changes.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — removing escalate_to_human during off-hours degrades service quality; it doesn't fix the over-escalation root cause.
whyWrongB: This is the misrouting-fix trap — adding a routing classifier is premature complexity when improving tool descriptions is the correct first intervention for misrouting.
whyWrongD: This is the any-vs-auto trap — tool_choice 'any' forces a tool call but doesn't guide the model toward the correct tool when descriptions are ambiguous.
examTrap: misrouting-fix: adds routing classifier instead of improving tool descriptions first

context: A developer uses Claude Code with a custom bash_executor MCP tool. A PostToolUse hook is configured to validate bash command outputs for security compliance — specifically to detect and log exfiltration patterns in command stdout. During a security audit, the team discovers the hook is logging command arguments correctly but has never logged a single stdout compliance violation in 4 months, despite manual testing confirming violations exist. The hook reads: tool.input.command to get the command string.
stem: What is the most likely reason the PostToolUse hook has never logged a stdout compliance violation?
optionA: PostToolUse hooks run in a sandboxed environment without access to tool output; compliance checks require a separate logging service.
optionB: The hook is reading tool.input.command (the command string passed to the tool) instead of tool.result.stdout (the tool's execution output) — it is checking the command for patterns instead of the stdout output.
optionC: PostToolUse fires before the bash command executes, so stdout is not yet available at the time of the hook's execution.

whyCorrect: PostToolUse fires AFTER tool execution with both the tool input AND the tool result available. The hook is accessing tool.input.command (what was sent to the tool) rather than tool.result.stdout (what the command printed). It's scanning command text for exfiltration patterns, not the actual output — explaining why no stdout violations are ever flagged.
whyWrongA: This is the partial-correct trap — PostToolUse hooks have full access to tool results; sandboxing does not prevent stdout access in this hook timing.
whyWrongC: This is the posttooluse-timing trap — PostToolUse fires AFTER execution by definition; stdout is fully available when the hook runs.
whyWrongD: This is the posttooluse-timing trap — PostToolUse fires before the model processes the result, not after; model processing timing is irrelevant to stdout availability.
examTrap: posttooluse-timing: confuses what data is available in PostToolUse hook context vs. what the hook is actually reading
